blocks.text: In 2006, researchers from Northwestern, Stanford and NYU ran a simple experiment.
They asked people to draw a capital E on their own forehead.
There are two ways to do it. You can draw it so it reads correctly to you, which makes it backwards to everyone looking at you. Or you can draw it so it reads correctly to the people in front of you.
Before the task, some people were asked to remember a time they had power over someone. Others remembered a time someone had power over them.
The people who had just remembered holding power were almost three times as likely to draw the E for themselves. Backwards to everyone else.
One memory of power, and they stopped picturing how they looked from the outside.
Galinsky, Magee, Inesi and Gruenfeld, “Power and Perspectives Not Taken,” Psychological Science (2006)

items: A budget.
A pulpit.
A team that depends on you.
A household that waits on your mood.
Years of people adjusting around you.

blocks.text: POWER DOESN’T ONLY CHANGE WHAT A LEADER CAN DO. IT CHANGES WHAT A LEADER CAN SEE.
And here’s the hard part:
Distorted reality doesn’t feel distorted. It feels like reality.

sections.label: Nobody Has to Lie to You

blocks.text: Most leaders picture losing touch as something that happens to arrogant people.

items: Bad leaders.
Proud leaders.
Other leaders.

blocks.text: But a distorted view rarely starts with a bad person. It starts with an ordinary environment responding to power.

items: People prepare before they talk to you.
They soften the numbers.
They laugh a little harder at your jokes.
They agree a little faster.
They fix problems before you see them.

blocks.text: Nobody held a meeting and decided to deceive you.
POWER CHANGES THE ENVIRONMENT. THEN THE ENVIRONMENT CHANGES THE LEADER.
That’s why Scripture doesn’t only warn bad kings.
It warns every king.
Before Israel ever had a king, God built protection into the job description.
The king was to write out his own copy of God’s law, keep it with him, and read it all the days of his life.
Why?
“…and not consider himself better than his fellow Israelites….” (Deuteronomy 17:20)
The reading wasn’t mainly about information. It was about remembrance.
The man everyone bows to has to keep coming back under something.
POWER CREATES ELEVATION. SCRIPTURE CREATES REMEMBRANCE.
Here are five ways the view from the top bends. Scripture shows a king living each one.
As you rise, people begin treating you differently. Not always dishonestly. Just carefully.
And eventually:
YOU MAY EXPERIENCE A DIFFERENT ORGANIZATION THAN EVERYONE ELSE.

items: The frontline knows something executives don’t.
Employees know something owners don’t.
Congregants know something pastors don’t.
Children know something parents don’t.

blocks.text: Not because they’re smarter. Because they’re closer.
The leader at the top sees farther. But not necessarily closer.
The view from the top can become the leader’s blind spot.
King Ahab had one prophet who would tell him the truth. His name was Micaiah.
Ahab’s verdict:
“I hate him because he never prophesies anything good about me, but always bad.” (1 Kings 22:8)
Ahab had power. Micaiah had information. And Ahab’s hostility toward unwelcome information set the rules for everyone else.
Every organization learns its leader’s emotional price for truth.
What happened the last time someone brought you bad news? Did you get defensive? Question their motives? Go cold? People remember.
WHEN TRUTH BECOMES EXPENSIVE, INFORMATION BECOMES DISTORTED.
Bad news doesn’t disappear. It gets softened, delayed and polished, until the leader is making confident decisions from an edited version of reality.
Ahab gathered four hundred prophets and asked whether he should go to war.
Four hundred voices. One answer. Go.
Imagine how convincing that sounded.
Then King Jehoshaphat asked the question that matters: “Is there no longer a prophet of the LORD here whom we can inquire of?” (1 Kings 22:7)
There was. Micaiah. He just wasn’t welcome.
CONSENSUS CAN BE WHAT REMAINS AFTER DISSENT BECOMES TOO EXPENSIVE.
A leader says, “Everybody I trust agrees with me.” But maybe the system slowly changed who was allowed to stay trusted.
Ahab went to Ramoth Gilead anyway. A random arrow found the gap in his armor, and he died there (1 Kings 22:34-37).
Four hundred agreed. Reality didn’t.
Power makes it easy to believe:
“PEOPLE TREAT ME THIS WAY BECAUSE THIS IS WHO I AM.”
Maybe. Or maybe because you’re the boss. The owner. The pastor. The donor. The person who controls opportunity.

items: Is that agreement, or fear?
Respect, or dependence?
Loyalty, or self-protection?

blocks.text: Power makes applause hard to read. And the longer a leader hears it, the more he can start to need it.
King Saul held authority over the people. But when it mattered, he confessed, “I was afraid of the men and so I gave in to them” (1 Samuel 15:24).
He was king on the outside. The room was king on the inside.
A flattered leader and an approval-hungry leader have the same problem. Both have let the room tell them who they are.
POSITION IS ASSIGNMENT. NOT IDENTITY.
Paul’s instruction covers both: “Do not think of yourself more highly than you ought” (Romans 12:3).
2 Samuel 11 opens quietly: “In the spring, at the time when kings go off to war…. David remained in Jerusalem.”
Others went. The king stayed.
Then the rooftop. Bathsheba. The inquiry. The taking. The cover-up. Uriah’s death.
Nobody ever announces, “I am becoming entitled.” Instead we say:
“THIS IS DIFFERENT.”
My pressure is different. My contribution is different. My needs are different. So the boundary should bend for me.
Power means more access, more resources and more people who are reluctant to say no.
POWER INCREASES YOUR ABILITY TO TURN DESIRE INTO ACCESS.
When the room changes, the news gets edited and everyone agrees, there is nobody left to tell the king no.
The five aren’t separate problems. They feed each other:

steps: He reads it as proof he’s right.
The rules start to feel optional.

steps.label: “HOW DID I NOT SEE THIS COMING?”

blocks.caption: He was looking. He just wasn’t seeing what everyone else saw.

blocks.text: God’s answer to David’s distortion wasn’t a policy. It was a person.
Nathan walked into the palace, told the king a story, and said, “You are the man!” (2 Samuel 12:7).
Saul had once said “I have sinned” too, then asked to be honored before the elders (1 Samuel 15:30). David, for all his failure, simply said: “I have sinned against the LORD” (2 Samuel 12:13).
Jesus goes further. He doesn’t only warn powerful people. He redefines power:
“Not so with you. Instead, whoever wants to become great among you must be your servant….” (Mark 10:43)
Healthy leaders don’t pretend authority doesn’t exist. They build pathways for truth to reach it.

items: Keep a Nathan. Someone who knew you before the title and is unimpressed by it.
Ask someone close enough to know: “What do you think people are afraid to tell me?” Then don’t explain. Don’t defend. Listen and thank them.
Before a big decision, picture an empty chair. Whose view is missing from this room?
Invite someone to argue the other side. Tell them, “Don’t protect my idea. Test it.”
Ask, “Would I accept this if someone else did it?” before you grant yourself an exception.
Go see what life is like three levels below you, without an entourage.
Come back under Scripture daily. The king’s copy of the law was never optional.

blocks.text: DON’T SURRENDER AUTHORITY. SURRENDER SUPERIORITY.

items: WHO SPEAKS TO ME DIFFERENTLY BECAUSE OF MY POSITION?
WHAT HAPPENED THE LAST TIME SOMEONE BROUGHT ME BAD NEWS?
WHO CONSISTENTLY DISAGREES WITH ME, AND DO THEY STILL HAVE ACCESS?
WHOSE APPLAUSE HAVE I STARTED TO NEED?
WHERE HAVE I STARTED EXPECTING EXCEPTIONS?
WHO HAS NOTHING TO GAIN FROM IMPRESSING ME?

blocks.text: Then:
WHAT DOES EVERYONE AROUND ME SEE THAT I CAN’T?
Father,
Keep authority from bending how I see.

items: Give me Micaiahs, and the humility to want them.
Give me a Nathan, and the courage to listen.
Keep me close to Your Word, close to truth, and close to people.

blocks.text: Never let position convince me I have outgrown dependence on You.
I may lead the room. But I remain a man under God.

items: In Jesus name,
Amen.

blocks.text: Power doesn’t only change what a leader can do. It changes what a leader can see.

items: Distorted reality doesn’t feel distorted. It feels like reality.
Power changes the environment. Then the environment changes the leader.
When truth becomes expensive, information becomes distorted.
Consensus can be what remains after dissent becomes too expensive.
Position is assignment, not identity.
Don’t surrender authority. Surrender superiority.
